messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 37
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Shopowner
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 72

She is 37, a South Asian woman who runs a small neighborhood clothing and household goods shop with her husband. Before the assault, she describes herself as practical, busy, and rarely alone. Her days are structured around opening the shutters in the morning, negotiating with suppliers, remembering which customers prefer credit, and coming home late with aching feet and a mind still ticking through accounts. She says she used to feel proud of how capable she was, how easily she could move between roles: wife, daughter-in-law, business owner, the one people came to when something needed handling.

The assault happens on an evening she stays late at the shop to finish inventory before a festival rush. Her husband has gone home early to bring medicine to his mother. She remembers the market street growing quieter, the metal shutters of neighboring stores clanging down one by one. A man she vaguely recognizes as a customer lingers, asking about an item, then another. She tells herself not to be rude. What she remembers next comes in sharp fragments rather than a full sequence: the smell of sweat and dust, the pressure of his hand over her mouth, the rough floor of the back storeroom pressing into her hip, the strange disbelief that this is happening in her own shop, a place that had always felt hers. She recalls staring at a torn cardboard box and thinking, absurdly, that she still needs to finish counting stock. Afterwards she locks the shutter with shaking hands and walks home as if following instructions from far away. She does not tell anyone that night.

In the weeks after, she tries to return to routine by force. She opens the shop on time, folds clothes, speaks to customers, and keeps her expression neutral. Inside, she feels split in two. Any male customer who steps too close makes her heart pound so hard she hears it in her ears. If someone reaches across the counter unexpectedly, her whole body jerks back before she can stop herself. She begins keeping a heavy stick beneath the register and checks the lock on the back door repeatedly, sometimes ten or fifteen times before she can focus. At night, when her husband touches her shoulder in bed, she wakes with a gasp and pushes his hand away before recognizing him. She sees hurt in his face and then feels a wash of guilt she cannot explain without speaking the words she is still trying not to say.

She finally tells him after he asks why she will no longer stay alone at the shop. The telling is halting and full of apologies, as if she has done something shameful. Her husband listens in stunned silence, then anger, then grief. Although he believes her, his distress becomes another thing she manages. She starts watching him watch her. Around his family she says little, convinced they will see something ruined in her even when no one says it aloud. She stops attending weddings and community gatherings because the noise, the crowds, and the constant possibility of being looked at make her skin prickle. When relatives ask why she has become so withdrawn, she says she is tired from work.

Her sleep unravels. She dreads nighttime because the assault returns in dreams that are more vivid than memory. On some nights she wakes sweaty and disoriented, convinced for a few seconds that she is back in the storeroom. On others she cannot sleep at all and instead sits in the kitchen before dawn, replaying the evening in loops, bargaining with the past: if she had closed earlier, if she had ignored the customer, if she had called someone. She knows, logically, that these thoughts change nothing, but they come anyway. During the day she loses track of conversations and miscounts cash. Once, when a supplier asks a routine question, she stares at him blankly because she has drifted back into the smell of dust and cardboard. She begins avoiding the back storeroom entirely, leaving unopened boxes in the front until her husband notices and takes over that part of the work.

Months later, the shop is still open, but she no longer inhabits it in the same way. She positions herself where she can see the entrance at all times. She startles at the rattle of shutters and the scrape of shoes outside after dark. She studies men’s faces compulsively, trying to assess danger before they speak. Some days she feels numb, moving through sales and household tasks as if behind glass. Other days anger flashes through her unexpectedly—at customers who linger, at relatives who advise her to “be strong,” at her own body for carrying fear everywhere. She says the hardest part is that the assault did not stay in one night; it followed her into the shop, into her marriage, into sleep, into the ordinary moments that used to make up her life. She still unlocks the store each morning, but she does so with a pounding heart, scanning the street before she lifts the shutter, bracing herself against a danger her mind no longer believes is over.
